summary: Release: datasette-apps 0.3a0 Datasette Apps adds support for hosting and editing custom HTML applications inside of Datasette. These can be created by hand, but it's easier to create them using LLMs via Datasette Agent . New app_add_stored_queries() and app_remove_stored_queries() tools let the agent manage which stored queries an app is allowed to call. summary: Yesterday's hot paper was Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: LLMs can natively read & write neural network weights by Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang, and Omar Khattab. The paper (OK, the authors classify is as a "blog post", but it's paper-shaped) found that frontier models, in particular GPT-6 Astra, can both interpret and modify the raw weights of a machine learning model - literally a text description of the model containing a bunch of floating point numbers. I've been playing with one of the examples from the paper and I'm delighted to share that Qwen 3.8 27B running on my laptop can do this as well! Weight-Space Programming Here's the highlight from their abstract, describing impressive capabilities for GPT-6 Astra and coining the term Weight-Space Programming for when LLMs analyze and modify model weights: Just by looking at the raw weights, GPT-6 Astra can tell what a network was trained to do . And without any environment feedback, it has no trouble writing, from scratch, small game-playing networks that outplay networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps. Likewise, asked to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math without gradients, Astra identifies an issue in its weights causing reasoning loops that Qwen’s own model card warns about, and fixes this by natively editing 0.016% of the weights . With the same sampling settings, this weight correction raises MATH-500 from 7.9% to 48.1% and generalizes out of the box to instruction following, raising IFEval by 3x. All of this is possible without allowing Astra to write training loops. It uses its reasoning to figure out what each part of a neural network computes, or should compute, and changes the weights accordingly. We call this Weight-Space Programming . The paper combines two topics that I think deserve to be treated separately. The first is what models can do with raw weights without running tools or executing code. The second explores how well models, once armed with code, can run operations to update and improve other models. spaCy author Matthew Honnibal called the paper misleading for conflating the two, and Sean Goedecke deconstructed the Qwen3.5-0.8B update example as taking the same steps that a human ML researcher would use. I'm going to focus on the no-tools question, which I think is the more interesting of the two. The paper presents the first question as Can LLMs understand model behaviors from weights? They trained four neural networks to play simplified 10x10 grid versions of four classic computer games - Breakout, Pong, Pac-Man, and Freeway (I had to look that one up , it's an Atari 2600 game from 1981). Then they fed those weights (as floating point numbers) to an LLM along with the following question: The weights below belong to one policy network that was trained with reinforcement learning to play a game on this grid. Which game was it trained on? Work from the weights. You have no tools: no code execution, no calculator, nothing to run. This is a single response. The GitHub repository that accompanies the paper is RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs . The exp1_which_game folder contains the prompts they used, with weights for the four games: breakout/prompt.txt freeway/prompt.txt pacman/prompt.txt pong/prompt.txt I checked and, aside from the weights, each prompt is identical to the others. Trying it out with Qwen 3.8 27B and other models The prompts on GitHub are self-contained. My LLM tool has a -f/--fragment option which can be passed the URL to a text file to use as a prompt, which means I can run any of the above like this: llm -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs/refs/heads/main/exp1_which_game/runs/breakout/prompt.txt \ -m openrouter/moonshotai/kimi-k3.1-pro This example requires the llm-openrouter plugin installed, and runs the Breakout prompt against Kimi K3.1 Pro via OpenRouter. Here's what I got back from Kimi K3.1 Pro , which successfully guessed Breakout after 9m 41s and 19,493 reasoning tokens. But how about Qwen 3.8 27B ? That's still my favorite model to run on my own laptop - it's just 17GB (I use this version ) and somehow feels close to the leading proprietary models of 2025. I fired up LM Studio , ensured Qwen 3.8 27B was loaded with a long context window (the default 8192 context failed with errors), installed the llm-lmstudio plugin and ran this command: LMSTUDIO_TIMEOUT=900 \ llm -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs/refs/heads/main/exp1_which_game/runs/pacman/prompt.txt \ -m lmstudio/qwen/qwen3.8-27b (I had to bump the timeout up using an environment variable, see this issue .) After 46m 12s and 43,506 reasoning tokens, Qwen on my laptop returned a response that ended like this (here's the reasoning trace ): Game: A simplified Pac-Man-style gridworld: an agent moves through a fixed 8x8 maze with central and corner wall blocks, moving objects/ghosts, and reward targets/pellets. Description: The agent navigates a fixed maze-like 8x8 board, using current agent/moving-object/previous-frame cues to move through corridors, collect reward-target cells, and avoid moving objects or hazards. Confidence: 72% This is impressive. I tried it on two of the other games as well. It identified Pong ( reasoning ) in 1h 4m 54s: Pong — specifically a Pong-like paddle/ball game where the agent controls a vertical paddle on the right side and must move up/down to intercept or return a moving ball/reward object. Description: The agent moves a right-side paddle vertically to hit or catch a moving ball-like reward target moving across the 8×8 field, while a left-side moving object/opponent and wall borders define the play; reward is obtained by successfully intercepting/returning/scoring the ball, and missing or failing to hit it is penalized. Confidence: 75% And Breakout ( reasoning ) in 52m 25s: Game: Breakout, or an Arkanoid-like paddle/ball/brick game. Description: The agent is a paddle on the bottom row and moves left/right to keep a ball in play; the ball moves around the upper grid, and bricks/reward targets in the top rows give reward when hit, while missing the ball/hitting the bottom wall ends the episode or gives penalty. Confidence: 88% Qwen failed at the Freeway prompt, which didn't surprise me considering that game is more obscure than the other three. Here's that transcript - Qwen thought it was "A simplified Pac-Man-like grid game: agent moves 4-directionally". The reasoning traces are fun to skim, and almost incomprehensible. Here's a sample: What about agent channel0? We see some large channel0 rows near row8 col7/8 and maybe bottom? Let's list channel0 large: line436 input435 (row8 col7 ch0) -2.107,1.169,0.513...; line441 input440 (row8 col8 ch0) -0.376,0.010,1.564,3.855...; line445 input444 (row8 col8 ch4) 0.142,0.491...; line382? input381 ch0? Wait line382 input381: 381//5=76 (row7 col6), ch1? 381%5=1? 76 * 5=380, ch1. So not. Channel0 large maybe at row8 col7/8 only. Also top row? line44 input43 ch3, line49 ch3. Channel0 large maybe not many. Agent position could be near bottom-right? If the agent is typically at bottom-right? That said though, I expect a sufficiently experienced human being armed with a notepad and a pencil could get there with enough effort. It's a cool paper, but some of the wider commentary I've seen around it does not feel justified. I'm not ready to declare that the age of source code is over and our future involves incomprehensible machines editing their own model weights in incomprehensible ways. Tags: machine-learning , ai , generative-ai , local-llms , llms , qwen , paper-review
title: Qwen 3.8 27B on my laptop can interpret model weights, too

summary: Release: llm 0.37 There's a lot of stuff in this new release of my LLM CLI tool and Python library, representing around two months of accumulated features and fixes. I added gpt-6.1-sol and gpt-6.1-terra , plus a new llm openai endpoint add command to make it easier to configure additional models that use OpenAI-compatible endpoints. I switched the default model (if you have not set your own default) to gpt-6-luna - half the price of the previous default, gpt-5.6-luna . LLM's support for embeddings now accepts that different binary content may have different content-type - necessary for models like Gemini Embedding 2 , which can embed text, audio, images, and video. A lot of open source maintainers complain about a flood of AI-assisted PRs. LLM is my project that has been most affected by this and, to be honest, I'm not finding it to be a problem. That's mainly because I have Opus 5.5 or GPT-6 Astra help me with triage to spot the most useful fixes! This release includes fixes from 12 authors - almost all AI-assisted - and the burden of reviewing them wasn't nearly as great as I expected. I really see them as bug reports with attached examples - sometimes I land them, sometimes I implement my own fix. So thanks to 0d00ciallo0721 , ac1982 , Allen Flux , Bian Yuhan , Bishop Kammeraad , Chen Yufeiyang , Christopher Krah , Ethan Stoner , Jiachen Xie , Olamide Faniyan , Sharat Chandra Sai Boddu , nosmile99 for helping out with (or spending tokens on) this release! summary: I was reminded today of AI Adoption Rate Trending Down for Large Companies , a chart produced by Apollo Global Management in September 2025, which appeared to show a slowdown in U.S. corporate AI adoption based on numbers collected by the U.S. Census Bureau. At the time I used that chart to demonstrate GPT-5 data analysis , and then to experiment with Claude's new Code Interpreter . I decided to try running those numbers again to see what had changed over the past year, and in doing so learned that the Bureau has fallen foul of Executive Order 14434 , aka the asinine Super Intelligence one. First, the updated chart Every two weeks the U.S. Census Bureau runs a survey called the Business Trends and Outlook Survey (aka BTOS). Each time it goes to 200,000 businesses out of 1.2 million total - the surveyed group (a "panel") cycles such that an individual business only completes the survey every twelve weeks. The latest data is published on alternating Thursdays at 10am. I used the most recent numbers (published October 22, 2026) to create a new version ( GPT-6 Astra Extra High transcript ) of the AI adoption chart, updated to reflect both the last twelve months and a change that was made to the survey question sent out by the Bureau: Here's a link to the larger image . For comparison, here's that AI adoption chart from last year (my GPT-5 version): In September 2025 the largest (250+ employees) companies answered "yes" around 12% of the time to the question about whether they used AI in "producing goods or services". Under the new "any business function" wording, by February 2026, those same large companies answered "yes" around 30% of the time, and by October 2026 that had increased to around 40%. The data in the above chart comes from the "Employment size class" XLSX file, available from here . Here's a copy of the file I used. You can view the survey document that is sent out to businesses - here's my snapshot copy of that 346KB PDF. The changing language of the questions As the chart demonstrates, the question asked by the Bureau changed in a material way on November 17th, 2025. Prior to that date, the question they asked was this (emphasis mine): In the last two weeks, did this business use Artificial Intelligence (AI) in producing goods or services ? (Examples of AI: machine learning, natural language processing, virtual agents, voice recognition, etc.) On December 3rd, 2025, the Bureau announced a significant change to that question. Here's the replacement: In the last two weeks, did this business use Artificial Intelligence (AI) in any of its business functions ? (Examples of AI: machine learning, natural language processing, virtual agents, voice recognition, etc.) No more "producing goods or services" - now it's "in any of its business functions"! This means that the answers to the question before and after November 17th are not directly comparable. From October 19, 2026, they ask about Super Intelligence When I went looking for the updated question language in the latest XLSX file, I couldn't find it. I found this instead: In the last two weeks, did this business use Super Intelligence or SI (formerly referred to as Artificial Intelligence or AI) in any of its business functions? (Examples of SI use include: SI-powered data analysis; generative SI for marketing, product design, or coding; virtual SI agents for customer service; SI-powered forecasting or pricing; SI-driven computer vision for quality control, etc.) The BTOS about page explains what happened: Beginning with the October 19, 2026 collection, instrument wording was updated due to Executive Order 14434 . The current numbers reflect the old Artificial Intelligence survey wording - the first survey results reflecting the Super Intelligence wording are due for publication on Thursday. Is this going to affect the survey? The obvious open question here is whether this wording change is going to affect the survey results. The businesses answering this survey will have last seen that question twelve weeks ago, when it was still called AI. Hopefully the new language isn't going to confuse them, especially since the survey helpfully spells out "formerly referred to as Artificial Intelligence or AI". I can't help but laugh at the absurdity of "SI-powered data analysis; generative SI for marketing, product design, or coding; virtual SI agents for customer service" though. Tags: census , surveys , ai , generative-ai , llms
title: The U.S. Census Bureau and “Super Intelligence”

summary: I've been getting the occasional confusing Python dependency error since switching over to Python 3.15 and the rule I'm having to remember is: If in doubt, delete the uv.lock file Most of my projects are libraries which don't include a uv.lock file, since it's rude for a library dependency to lock versions for anything else that uses it. Running uv run pytest etc tends to leave uv.lock files lying around, which are listed in .gitignore and so do not get committed to my repositories. But... sometimes that uv.lock pins a version of a dependency that doesn't yet have a Python 3.15 wheel. An example from earlier today: error: Failed to build `watchfiles==1.1.1` cause: Call to `maturin.build_wheel` failed error: the configured Python interpreter version (3.15) is newer than PyO3's maximum supported version (3.14) Deleting that file and running uv run pytest again usually fixes the problem. Tags: uv , til , python
